news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Universal HPV vaccination and anal cancer screening take centre stage in push to eliminate HPV-associated cancers by October 28, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Universal HPV vaccination and anal cancer screening take centre stage in push to eliminate HPV-associated cancers Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Experts convened by the HPV Prevention and Control Board at its 18th technical meeting in Antwerp, Belgium, in June 2025 concluded that eliminating HPV-associated cancers will require extending prevention beyond the traditional focus on cervical cancer in women, combining universal HPV vaccination that includes boys with targeted anal cancer screening for the populations at highest risk. The meeting report, published in BMC Proceedings, synthesises the epidemiology, modelling evidence and country experiences discussed at the meeting. The case for including men rests on a substantial and growing burden of disease. HPV causes approximately 148,072 cancer cases in men annually worldwide, a figure the meeting’s participants described as likely a substantial undercount, with conservative re-estimates suggesting around 180,000 cases per year. These cancers affect primarily the oropharynx, anus and penis. Oropharyngeal cancer is the most common HPV-associated malignancy in men, and incidence among males in high-income countries has more than doubled over the past 15 years, now exceeding that of cervical cancer in women; men are five times more likely to be diagnosed than women. Age-standardised incidence rates per 100,000 are highest in North America at 6.0, Europe at 5.5 and Oceania at 5.3. Discover more Book Lab Tests Book Care Services Vaccine Biological differences between sexes reinforce the argument for vaccinating boys. Men have lower seroconversion rates than women following natural genital HPV infection, suggesting prolonged susceptibility, and unlike in women, in whom HPV prevalence declines with age, oral and genital HPV prevalence in men remains relatively constant across age groups. Data from 64 studies covering approximately 29,900 men show wide variability in anal high-risk HPV prevalence by risk group: 74.3 percent among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men living with HIV, 41.2 percent among HIV-negative men who have sex with men, and 6.9 percent in HIV-negative men who have sex with women. Discover more Find Cancer Care Cancer cancer cancers Direct trial evidence supports the superiority of universal over girls-only vaccination. Between 2007 and 2014, a community-randomised trial across 33 Finnish communities enrolled over 80,000 adolescents, randomising them to universal HPV16/18 vaccination, girls-only HPV16/18 vaccination or control hepatitis B vaccination, with overall coverage of 52 percent in girls and 29 percent in boys. In communities where both boys and girls were vaccinated, HPV16/18 prevalence was significantly reduced not only among vaccinated but also among unvaccinated females, and the herd effect was stronger in the universal arms than in girls-only arms. Prevalence of other high-risk types, including HPV18, 31, 33 and 35, was also markedly lower in the universal vaccination group. By contrast, girls-only and lower-coverage arms offered limited herd protection, leaving unvaccinated and marginalised women disproportionately affected. The meeting heard that even moderate-coverage universal vaccination can deliver substantial public health benefits within five years, and that modelling and ecological observations suggest elimination of the most oncogenic types, HPV16 and 18, may be feasible within 15 to 30 years if universal strategies are widely adopted. Modelling analyses nonetheless identify high coverage in girls as the most efficient strategy for cervical cancer elimination specifically. The HPV-ADVISE transmission-dynamic model, calibrated to six core countries and mapped to 67 low- and middle-income countries and 40 high-income countries, found routine single-dose vaccination of 9-year-old girls to be the most efficient strategy, with adding boys offering limited additional benefit because of herd immunity conferred by high coverage in girls. Increasing coverage in girls from 40 to 80 percent yielded up to three times the reduction in cervical cancer cases compared with initiating vaccination in boys at the same coverage level. However, meeting participants stressed that cost-effectiveness is necessary but not sufficient for policy decisions: when equity, acceptability, programme resilience and the prevention of non-cervical cancers are incorporated, universal vaccination is justified on broader public health grounds, including reducing the projected incidence gap between low- and middle-income and high-income countries. Discover more Book a Checkup Find Vaccines Check Symptoms Global implementation remains uneven. By 2025, 149 of 194 countries had introduced HPV vaccine into national immunisation schedules, but 55 percent of girls worldwide still live in countries without an HPV vaccination programme. Average first-dose coverage rose modestly from 55 percent in 2021 to 62 percent in 2023, and only 16 countries achieved greater than 90 percent first-dose national coverage in 2023. The adoption of the WHO-recommended single-dose schedule has accelerated scale-up, with approximately 28 million girls and 6 million boys aged 9 to 14 receiving a first dose in 2023. Supply dynamics are shifting, with new manufacturers and technology transfers reshaping the market, and supply projected to stabilise at around 100 million doses annually, potentially peaking at 130 million under universal vaccination. Country experiences presented at the meeting highlighted persistent equity gaps. In Scotland, where the school-based programme was introduced for girls in 2008 and extended to boys in 2019, uptake remains uneven: among pupils in the fourth year of secondary school in 2024/25, coverage was 75 percent in the most deprived areas compared with 91 percent in the least deprived, a gap that has increased substantially since the programme was extended to boys. In Cameroon, early pilot programmes demonstrated strong community engagement, with 74 percent of girls in Foumban and Edéa completing both doses, but the 2020 national rollout faced strong resistance from religious leaders and some healthcare professionals, and two years after launch 84 percent of health facilities were not offering HPV vaccination. A revamped strategy combining a single-dose schedule, extension to boys, periodic intensification of routine immunisation and renewed community partnerships improved coverage across all regions, with four regions reaching over 90 percent coverage in girls and around 40 percent in boys, although the report notes that the concurrent interventions make it difficult to attribute coverage gains to any single measure. On secondary prevention, the meeting identified anal cancer screening as the most advanced non-cervical strategy warranting immediate attention. The pivotal ANCHOR study, a randomised controlled trial involving more than 10,000 individuals with HIV, demonstrated that treating biopsy-proven anal high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions through office-based electrocautery reduced progression to anal cancer by 57 percent compared with active monitoring. Notably, 53 percent of men, 47 percent of women and 67 percent of transgender individuals screened were diagnosed with high-grade lesions, highlighting the high prevalence of precancerous lesions in these populations. In the monitoring arm, progression from high-grade lesions to cancer occurred at a rate of 400 per 100,000 person-years, and the risk of progression was 5.26-fold higher for lesions involving more than 50 percent of the anal or perianal canal compared with smaller lesions, providing an early basis for lesion-based risk stratification. Implementation of anal screening remains constrained despite the publication in 2024 of the first evidence-based guidelines from the U.S. Health and Human Services and the International Anal Neoplasia Society. Barriers include limited high-resolution anoscopy capacity, workforce shortages, stigma, and limited evidence on optimal screening algorithms, with all current screening recommendations based on expert opinion rather than prospective evidence. In the United States, only 22 percent of people in HIV care received care at facilities with on-site high-resolution anoscopy, and one-third attended clinics with no known access to such services. Experiences from Puerto Rico, where over 1,400 patients have been evaluated at the Anal Neoplasia Clinic of the University of Puerto Rico Comprehensive Cancer Centre since 2014, and from Belgium, where an estimated 9,500 people living with HIV aged over 50 and up to 235,000 men who have sex with men and transwomen over 45 may require regular screening, illustrate both the growing demand and the bottlenecks in trained personnel and coordination. The meeting concluded that integrating universal vaccination with targeted anal cancer screening, supported by equitable access, biomarker development, self-sampling approaches and living guidelines that evolve with emerging evidence, is essential to reducing the HPV-related cancer burden in both women and men. Participants emphasised that vaccinating boys will not protect hard-to-reach girls, since people often partner within their ethnic or social circles where similar barriers to vaccination exist, and that sustained investment in communication, community engagement and workforce training will be required to translate these strategies into population-level impact. Discover more Find Cancer Care Cancer cancer cancers Direct trial evidence supports the superiority of universal over girls-only vaccination. Between 2007 and 2014, a community-randomised trial across 33 Finnish communities enrolled over 80,000 adolescents, randomising them to universal HPV16/18 vaccination, girls-only HPV16/18 vaccination or control hepatitis B vaccination, with overall coverage of 52 percent in girls and 29 percent in boys. In communities where both boys and girls were vaccinated, HPV16/18 prevalence was significantly reduced not only among vaccinated but also among unvaccinated females, and the herd effect was stronger in the universal arms than in girls-only arms. Prevalence of other high-risk types, including HPV18, 31, 33 and 35, was also markedly lower in the universal vaccination group. By contrast, girls-only and lower-coverage arms offered limited herd protection, leaving unvaccinated and marginalised women disproportionately affected. The meeting heard that even moderate-coverage universal vaccination can deliver substantial public health benefits within five years, and that modelling and ecological observations suggest elimination of the most oncogenic types, HPV16 and 18, may be feasible within 15 to 30 years if universal strategies are widely adopted. Modelling analyses nonetheless identify high coverage in girls as the most efficient strategy for cervical cancer elimination specifically. The HPV-ADVISE transmission-dynamic model, calibrated to six core countries and mapped to 67 low- and middle-income countries and 40 high-income countries, found routine single-dose vaccination of 9-year-old girls to be the most efficient strategy, with adding boys offering limited additional benefit because of herd immunity conferred by high coverage in girls. Increasing coverage in girls from 40 to 80 percent yielded up to three times the reduction in cervical cancer cases compared with initiating vaccination in boys at the same coverage level. However, meeting participants stressed that cost-effectiveness is necessary but not sufficient for policy decisions: when equity, acceptability, programme resilience and the prevention of non-cervical cancers are incorporated, universal vaccination is justified on broader public health grounds, including reducing the projected incidence gap between low- and middle-income and high-income countries. Discover more Book a Checkup Find Vaccines Check Symptoms Global implementation remains uneven. By 2025, 149 of 194 countries had introduced HPV vaccine into national immunisation schedules, but 55 percent of girls worldwide still live in countries without an HPV vaccination programme. Average first-dose coverage rose modestly from 55 percent in 2021 to 62 percent in 2023, and only 16 countries achieved greater than 90 percent first-dose national coverage in 2023. The adoption of the WHO-recommended single-dose schedule has accelerated scale-up, with approximately 28 million girls and 6 million boys aged 9 to 14 receiving a first dose in 2023. Supply dynamics are shifting, with new manufacturers and technology transfers reshaping the market, and supply projected to stabilise at around 100 million doses annually, potentially peaking at 130 million under universal vaccination. Country experiences presented at the meeting highlighted persistent equity gaps. In Scotland, where the school-based programme was introduced for girls in 2008 and extended to boys in 2019, uptake remains uneven: among pupils in the fourth year of secondary school in 2024/25, coverage was 75 percent in the most deprived areas compared with 91 percent in the least deprived, a gap that has increased substantially since the programme was extended to boys. In Cameroon, early pilot programmes demonstrated strong community engagement, with 74 percent of girls in Foumban and Edéa completing both doses, but the 2020 national rollout faced strong resistance from religious leaders and some healthcare professionals, and two years after launch 84 percent of health facilities were not offering HPV vaccination. A revamped strategy combining a single-dose schedule, extension to boys, periodic intensification of routine immunisation and renewed community partnerships improved coverage across all regions, with four regions reaching over 90 percent coverage in girls and around 40 percent in boys, although the report notes that the concurrent interventions make it difficult to attribute coverage gains to any single measure. On secondary prevention, the meeting identified anal cancer screening as the most advanced non-cervical strategy warranting immediate attention. The pivotal ANCHOR study, a randomised controlled trial involving more than 10,000 individuals with HIV, demonstrated that treating biopsy-proven anal high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions through office-based electrocautery reduced progression to anal cancer by 57 percent compared with active monitoring. Notably, 53 percent of men, 47 percent of women and 67 percent of transgender individuals screened were diagnosed with high-grade lesions, highlighting the high prevalence of precancerous lesions in these populations. In the monitoring arm, progression from high-grade lesions to cancer occurred at a rate of 400 per 100,000 person-years, and the risk of progression was 5.26-fold higher for lesions involving more than 50 percent of the anal or perianal canal compared with smaller lesions, providing an early basis for lesion-based risk stratification. Implementation of anal screening remains constrained despite the publication in 2024 of the first evidence-based guidelines from the U.S. Health and Human Services and the International Anal Neoplasia Society. Barriers include limited high-resolution anoscopy capacity, workforce shortages, stigma, and limited evidence on optimal screening algorithms, with all current screening recommendations based on expert opinion rather than prospective evidence. In the United States, only 22 percent of people in HIV care received care at facilities with on-site high-resolution anoscopy, and one-third attended clinics with no known access to such services. Experiences from Puerto Rico, where over 1,400 patients have been evaluated at the Anal Neoplasia Clinic of the University of Puerto Rico Comprehensive Cancer Centre since 2014, and from Belgium, where an estimated 9,500 people living with HIV aged over 50 and up to 235,000 men who have sex with men and transwomen over 45 may require regular screening, illustrate both the growing demand and the bottlenecks in trained personnel and coordination. The meeting concluded that integrating universal vaccination with targeted anal cancer screening, supported by equitable access, biomarker development, self-sampling approaches and living guidelines that evolve with emerging evidence, is essential to reducing the HPV-related cancer burden in both women and men. Participants emphasised that vaccinating boys will not protect hard-to-reach girls, since people often partner within their ethnic or social circles where similar barriers to vaccination exist, and that sustained investment in communication, community engagement and workforce training will be required to translate these strategies into population-level impact. analysis.location_and_population: The meeting took place in Antwerp, Belgium. The analysis covers global populations, with specific mention of high-income countries and regions such as North America, Europe, and Oceania. It also highlights populations at risk, including men who have sex with men (MSM), particularly those living with HIV, and girls and boys in various countries.
analysis.event: Experts convened by the HPV Prevention and Control Board concluded that eliminating HPV-associated cancers requires extending prevention beyond cervical cancer in women, combining universal HPV vaccination that includes boys with targeted anal cancer screening for high-risk populations. This is based on epidemiological data, modeling evidence, and country experiences.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: HPV causes approximately 148,072 cancer cases in men annually worldwide, with conservative re-estimates suggesting around 180,000 cases per year. These cancers primarily affect the oropharynx, anus, and penis. Oropharyngeal cancer is the most common HPV-associated malignancy in men, with incidence rates in high-income countries more than doubling over the past 15 years. The report also notes that universal vaccination strategies could reduce the incidence gap between low- and middle-income countries and high-income countries.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The meeting discussed the need for universal HPV vaccination and anal cancer screening. A community-randomised trial in Finland showed that universal vaccination significantly reduced HPV16/18 prevalence. The WHO-recommended single-dose schedule has been adopted, with 28 million girls and 6 million boys aged 9 to 14 receiving a first dose in 2023. However, implementation remains uneven, and supply dynamics are shifting. The report also highlights equity gaps in coverage, such as in Scotland and Cameroon.

The report also notes that anal cancer screening is the most advanced non-cervical strategy, but its implementation is constrained. The analysis is based on epidemiological data, modeling evidence, and country experiences, with the goal of achieving broader public health benefits and reducing the incidence gap between different income levels.

news.content_title: South Africa’s HPV Vaccination Drive to Protect Girls from Cervical Cancer is Working – What We Know After 10 Years
news.content: South Africa’s school-based HPV vaccination programme is delivering measurable population-level benefits. By The Conversation First published October 19, 2026 by The Conversation and reprinted October 22, 2026 by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance/VaccinesWork South Africa introduced a vaccination for human papillomavirus (HPV) in public schools in 2014. The programme offered the vaccination to grade 4 girls aged nine years and older. Uptake was high from the start. About 87% of eligible girls received at least one dose during the first year. Almost all cervical cancers are caused by persistent infection with HPV, a very common virus transmitted through sexual contact. Most HPV infections clear naturally, but some high-risk types can persist and can eventually lead to cervical cancer. HPV types 16 and 18 alone are responsible for around 70% of cervical cancer cases worldwide. Cervical cancer is one of the most preventable forms of cancer, yet it remains a major cause of illness and death among women worldwide. Each year, more than 660,000 women are diagnosed globally, and over 90% of new cases and deaths caused by cervical cancer happen in low- and middle-income countries. The challenge is particularly acute in South Africa because HIV increases the risk of HPV infection persisting and progressing to cervical disease. Women living with HIV are much more likely to develop cervical cancer during their lifetime than women without HIV. South Africa had an estimated 7.9 million people living with HIV in mid-2025, accounting for 12.3% of the total population. We are public health researchers dedicated to advancing prevention and treatment of sexually transmitted infections. We evaluated the 2014 vaccination programme’s impact on HPV prevalence among adolescent girls in a setting of high HIV prevalence in South Africa. Our findings were striking. They showed that: - infections with HPV types 16 and 18 fell by 83% between pre-vaccine and post-vaccine groups - infections with the HPV types responsible for most cervical cancers have fallen by more than 80% among adolescent girls eligible for vaccination, including those living with HIV. This is encouraging news for a country that carries one of the world’s highest burdens of cervical cancer. It also provides important evidence for other African countries with high HIV prevalence that are working towards eliminating cervical cancer as a public health problem. Measuring the impact Because cervical cancer can take decades to develop after HPV infection, it is still too early to measure the programme’s success by looking at cancer rates alone. Instead, our research examined whether vaccine-targeted HPV infections are becoming less common among vaccine-programme eligible generations. A substantial reduction in these infections is a strong early sign that future cervical cancer rates will fall. To assess the programme’s impact, we conducted the HPV One and Two Dose Population Effectiveness (HOPE) study in 2019 and 2023. We compared how common HPV was among adolescent girls aged 17-18 years who were too old to receive the HPV vaccine when the national programme began, with girls of the same age who had been eligible for vaccination through the school-based programme. The study included 2,357 participants recruited from public healthcare facilities across four South African provinces. Importantly, about one-quarter of participants were living with HIV. This allowed us to examine vaccine impact in a population that faces a higher risk of cervical cancer. Our findings Across all participants, infections with HPV types 16 and 18 fell by 83% between pre-vaccine and post-vaccine groups. Before the vaccination programme, about one in five girls carried one of these high-risk HPV types. Among girls eligible for vaccination, that number fell to approximately three in every 100 girls. The programme performed equally well among girls living with HIV. In this group, HPV 16/18 infections fell from 29% to 4%, representing an 82% reduction. We also observed reductions in high-risk HPV types that are genetically related to HPV 16 and 18, a phenomenon known as cross-protection. This increased the overall impact of the vaccination programme. At the same time, other HPV types did not fall. This strengthens confidence that the observed reductions were due to vaccination, not other factors such as changes in sexual behaviour. Another important finding was evidence of indirect protection also known as “herd protection”. Girls in the post-vaccine era who had no documented record of being vaccinated, or did not report having been vaccinated, had much lower rates of HPV 16 and 18 than girls in the pre-vaccine group. This suggests that when most people are vaccinated, the virus spreads much less in the wider community, helping protect unvaccinated individuals. What this means for South Africa and the region The findings provide compelling evidence that South Africa’s HPV vaccination programme is achieving its primary goal: preventing infections that would otherwise place young women at risk of developing cervical cancer later in life. They also demonstrate that the benefits extend to adolescent girls living with HIV, a group that stands to gain substantially from effective cervical cancer prevention. This is especially important for countries in eastern and southern Africa, where both HIV and cervical cancer remain major public health challenges. In 2022, the World Health Organization recommended a single-dose HPV vaccine for the general population, with the aim of simplifying delivery and increasing global coverage for settings that need it most. Since October 2024, South Africa has adopted a single-dose HPV vaccination approach. Continued monitoring will be important to ensure long-term protection, particularly among people living with HIV. A decade after its introduction, the country’s school-based HPV vaccination programme is delivering measurable population-level benefits and providing a model for other countries seeking to prevent one of the world’s most avoidable cancers. Website This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article. Authors Dorothy Nyemba-Machemedze, Data Analyst – Epidemiologist/Biostatistician at Wits RHI, University of the Witwatersrand and Sinead Delany-Moretlwe, Associate Professor and Director: Research at the Wits Reproductive Health and HIV Institute I, University of the Witwatersrand Related Articles England’s NHS Rolls out Discreet Cervical Cancer Home-Testing Kits for Millions of Women Nearly four million women who’ve missed screening invitations will be offered free HPV self-testing swabs to complete at home, part of NHS England’s push to increase screening and eliminate cervical cancer entirely by 2040. Fewer Young Women Are Dying of Cervical Cancer in England A landmark study found no cervical cancer deaths among women aged 20 to 24 in England from 2020 to 2024, the first direct evidence that HPV vaccination saves lives, not just prevents infections. Researchers estimate it has already prevented roughly 200 deaths. Student Champions in Mozambique Promote HPV Vaccination in the Fight to Prevent Cervical Cancer In Mozambique, VillageReach’s INTEGRATE HPV initiative is reshaping cervical cancer prevention. When trained teachers and student peer champions led the conversation, fear gave way to enthusiasm. School-based HPV vaccinations surged nearly tenfold across intervention sites

analysis.time: The HPV vaccination programme was introduced in 2014, and the study was conducted in 2019 and 2023. The findings were reported in 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: South Africa, specifically among adolescent girls aged 17-18 years, with about one-quarter of participants living with HIV.
analysis.event: South Africa’s school-based HPV vaccination programme has shown measurable population-level benefits in reducing infections with high-risk HPV types, particularly HPV 16 and 18, among adolescent girls, including those living with HIV. The study was conducted by public health researchers.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: HPV 16 and 18 infections fell by 83% among vaccinated girls and 82% among girls living with HIV. These reductions are significant and suggest a strong impact on preventing cervical cancer. The programme's success is highlighted as a model for other countries.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The programme is ongoing, and continued monitoring is important to ensure long-term protection, especially among people living with HIV. The study findings are based on population-level data and are considered encouraging but require further observation.

analysis.brief_en: South Africa’s school-based HPV vaccination programme, introduced in 2014, has demonstrated measurable benefits in reducing infections with high-risk HPV types, particularly HPV 16 and 18, among adolescent girls. A study conducted in 2019 and 2023 found that these infections fell by 83% in vaccinated groups and 82% in girls living with HIV. The programme's success is attributed to its impact on preventing cervical cancer, which remains a major health issue in the country. The findings suggest that the programme is effective in reducing the risk of cervical cancer, even in high-risk populations. Continued monitoring is essential to ensure long-term protection, especially for those living with HIV. The study highlights the importance of HPV vaccination in public health and serves as a model for other countries facing similar challenges.

news.content_zh: 南非于 2014 年推出的以学校为基础的 HPV 疫苗接种 计划已证明在减少青春期女孩中 高危型HPV 类型(特别是 HPV 16 和 18 型)感染方面具有显着的效益。2019 年和 2023 年进行的一项研究发现,接种疫苗的群体的感染率下降了 83%,感染艾滋病毒的女孩的感染率下降了 82%。该计划的成功归功于其对预防 宫颈癌 的影响,宫颈癌 仍然是该国的一个主要健康问题。研究结果表明,该计划可以有效降低 宫颈癌 的风险,即使是在高危人群中也是如此。持续监测对于确保长期保护至关重要,特别是对于艾滋病毒感染者。该研究强调了 HPV 疫苗接种 在公共卫生中的重要性,并为面临类似挑战的其他国家提供了借鉴。

news.content_title: HPV prevention, local action drive push for a cervical cancer-free Philippines
news.content: CERVICAL cancer is one of the few cancers the world has set out to eliminate as a public health problem. For the Philippines, however, reaching that goal will depend not only on national targets but on whether prevention actually reaches girls and women in their communities. At the center of prevention is the human papillomavirus (HPV), a common virus transmitted through sexual contact. While most HPV infections clear on their own, persistent infection with high-risk HPV types can lead to cervical cancer. Around 95 percent of cervical cancer cases are linked to persistent high-risk HPV infection, making HPV vaccination an important opportunity to prevent the disease before it develops, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The WHO has set a 90-70-90 strategy toward cervical cancer elimination by 2030: 90 percent of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15, 70 percent of women screened with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45, and 90 percent of women identified with cervical disease receiving treatment. At the recent Association of Municipal Health Officers of the Philippines symposium on “Leading Disease Prevention at the Local Level: The Role of LGUs in Protecting Communities,” health experts brought the global target closer to home: how can proven prevention measures translate into protection that people can actually access in their barangays, municipalities and cities? Closing the gaps in HPV vaccination Get the latest news delivered to your inbox Sign up for The Manila Times newsletters By signing up with an email address, I acknowledge that I have read and agree to the Terms of Service and Privacy Policy . Pediatric Infectious Disease Specialist Dr. Fejelia Faulan, resource speaker and panelist, emphasized that gaps in HPV vaccination cannot be traced to one factor alone. Families, health care providers, schools and communities can all influence whether eligible children ultimately receive protection. ADVOCATING HPV VACCINATION Dr. Fejelia Faulan discusses the role of HPV vaccination and stronger local implementation in accelerating the Philippines’ progress toward cervical cancer elimination. “The gaps are on many sides,” Faulan said, pointing to challenges ranging from parental and community attitudes to vaccine access and hesitancy. She noted that misinformation and resistance to vaccination can make reaching eligible populations particularly difficult. Another important gap is data. While government vaccination programs capture vaccinations delivered through the public sector, Faulan noted that there is no comprehensive national registry capturing HPV vaccination delivered through private practice. In Western Visayas, members of the Philippine Pediatric Society have started gathering vaccination information from private practitioners, which Faulan said could help provide a more complete picture of coverage. “We started that program because we wanted to share our data with the government; so that we can address and minimize the gap,” Faulan said. “We hope that there will be others, other municipalities who will join, so that it can become national data for private practitioners.” The issue goes beyond measurement. If local governments do not know how many children have already been vaccinated through private clinics and schools, it becomes harder to identify who is still being missed and where resources should be directed. Faulan also underscored the importance of widening vaccination reach. The current government program prioritizes girls aged 9 to 14, but she noted that HPV infection is not exclusively a concern for women. HPV can also cause cancers affecting men, including anal, penile and oropharyngeal cancers. WHO likewise recognizes HPV as a cause of several cancers beyond cervical cancer. Local success stories show that ambitious vaccination targets are achievable. During the symposium, Faulan highlighted areas that have reached the 90 percent HPV vaccination target, including Banna in Ilocos Norte and Sampaloc, Quezon, while Ilocos Norte subsequently achieved the target province-wide. “If Ilocos Norte has done this, and one municipality in Quezon has done this, I think we can do this,” Faulan told local health leaders. Making prevention a sustained local priority For Dr. Debra Maria Catulong, city health officer of Mandaue City and Best-Practice Panelist, closing the gap requires LGUs to shift their thinking from detecting disease to preventing it in the first place. “Why are we waiting for people to get sick and diagnose or screen? Why can’t we do something before that?” Catulong said, describing Mandaue City's move toward prevention under the primary healthcare approach. CERVICAL CANCER PREVENTION Dr. Debra Maria Catulong shares Mandaue City’s approach to strengthening cervical cancer prevention through local planning, sustainable financing and expanded HPV vaccination.PHOTO FROM The city is putting this into practice through a cervical cancer prevention initiative designed to complement the national program. While government-supplied HPV vaccines reach eligible girls through the public sector, Mandaue City has allocated local resources to extend vaccination to girls aged 9 to 14 in private schools, helping address a population that may otherwise be missed. The city is also working to establish a mechanism for capturing private-sector vaccination data to better understand its actual coverage. For Catulong, however, vaccination campaigns should not become one-time activities. Sustainable prevention requires LGUs to formally incorporate cervical cancer elimination into their annual plans and identify resources that can support implementation over time. Mandaue City, for instance, is augmenting its health budget through several sources, including its general fund, Special Health Fund and Gender and Development Fund. “Marami kayong pwedeng ma-source out na funds. Ang importante lang, the willingness, awareness and acknowledgement na gusto mong ipasok ’yan na budget should be coming from us,” Catulong told municipal health officers. She added that local strategies should combine vaccination with health promotion and navigation for patients already diagnosed, while tapping private companies, civil society organizations and other partners within the community. “It should be something that’s sustainable. As much as possible, embed it in the plans annually,” Catulong said. “Hindi kaya ito ng isang sektor lang. We all need to work together if we really want to eliminate cervical cancer.” That approach reflects one of the central lessons emerging from the symposium: national targets become meaningful only when they are translated into local plans, budgets and services. Science has already established a pathway toward cervical cancer elimination. Closing the remaining gap will increasingly depend on knowing who is still being missed, making vaccination accessible across public and private settings, sustaining local financing and building partnerships that can carry prevention beyond individual campaigns. For LGUs, the opportunity is to turn the 90-70-90 targets from national numbers into something more tangible: girls protected from HPV today, and fewer women facing cervical cancer in the years ahead

news.content_zh: 文章重点介绍了菲律宾通过 HPV 预防消除 宫颈癌 的努力,重点关注当地行动和实施。它强调了 HPV 疫苗接种 在预防 宫颈癌 方面的重要性,并指出约 95% 的病例与持续性 高危型HPV 感染有关。世卫组织的 90-70-90 战略目标是到 15 岁实现 90% 的 疫苗接种 覆盖率,对 35-45 岁的女性实现 70% 的筛查,对确诊患者实现 90% 的 治疗 覆盖率。曼达维市等地方政府正在努力将 疫苗接种 扩展到私立学校,并从私人从业者那里收集数据,以解决覆盖范围的差距。卫生专家强调,当地需要持续努力,包括将消除 宫颈癌 纳入年度计划并通过多种来源获得资金。该文章强调了社区参与、意识和合作的重要性,以确保公共和私营部门的预防措施可及且有效。

news.content: Advanced Search Home News Releases Multimedia Meetings Login Register News Release 29-Oct-2026 HPV-driven cell death pathways offer new directions for cervical cancer treatment “This review proposes that PCD in cervical cancer should be understood not as a series of isolated pathways, but as an interconnected regulatory network that governs both tumor behavior and therapeutic sensitivity” Peer-Reviewed Publication Impact Journals LLC Facebook X LinkedIn WeChat Bluesky Message WhatsApp Email image: Figure 4. Schematic representation illustrating the multifaceted role of programmed cell death pathways in the diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of cervical cancer. view more Credit: Copyright: © 2026 Kumar. This is an open access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY 4.0), which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original author and source are credited. “This review proposes that PCD in cervical cancer should be understood not as a series of isolated pathways, but as an interconnected regulatory network that governs both tumor behavior and therapeutic sensitivity.” BUFFALO, NY — October 29, 2026 — A new review was published in Volume 13 of Oncoscience on September 30, 2026, titled “Programmed cell death pathways in cervical cancer: Cross-talk, HPV-mediated regulation, and therapeutic implications: A narrative review.” The review examines how human papillomavirus (HPV) alters programmed cell death pathways in cervical cancer, allowing malignant cells to survive, evade immune responses and develop resistance to treatment. By exploring interactions among different cell death mechanisms, the article highlights potential therapeutic strategies to restore cancer-cell susceptibility to destruction and improve responses to existing treatments. However, most emerging approaches remain experimental and require clinical validation. The review was authored by Naina Kumar, affiliated with the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Bibinagar, Hyderabad, India. Cervical cancer remains a major global health challenge, with persistent infection by high-risk HPV types, particularly HPV16 and HPV18, representing its principal cause. Although vaccination, screening and advances in treatment have improved prevention and care, patients with advanced or recurrent disease continue to face treatment resistance and limited therapeutic options. Programmed cell death (PCD) is a biological process through which damaged, abnormal or unnecessary cells are eliminated through regulated molecular mechanisms. These pathways help maintain tissue health and prevent uncontrolled growth. Cancer cells, however, can interfere with these processes, allowing them to survive despite genetic damage or exposure to anticancer treatments. The review synthesizes literature published through October 2025, drawing on studies identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science. It examines how different forms of programmed cell death interact with HPV-related signaling, the tumor microenvironment and emerging therapeutic strategies. A central focus is apoptosis, the best-characterized form of programmed cell death. This process removes damaged cells through coordinated molecular events involving proteins such as BAX, BCL-2 and caspases. However, cervical cancer cells frequently suppress these signals, allowing them to resist chemotherapy, radiation and other treatments. High-risk HPV contributes directly to this resistance through two viral proteins, E6 and E7. E6 promotes degradation of p53, a tumor-suppressor protein that normally helps trigger apoptosis in damaged cells. This reduces the activity of pro-apoptotic molecules such as BAX, PUMA and NOXA. Meanwhile, E7 interferes with the retinoblastoma (RB) pathway, disrupting normal cell-cycle control and promoting uncontrolled proliferation. Together, these mechanisms support cancer-cell survival while influencing other forms of programmed cell death. The review emphasizes that overcoming HPV-associated resistance may require targeting several interconnected pathways rather than restoring apoptosis alone. One promising alternative is ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death caused by the accumulation of damaging lipid peroxides. Unlike apoptosis, ferroptosis depends strongly on iron metabolism, oxidative stress and antioxidant defenses involving proteins such as GPX4 and SLC7A11. Disrupting these protective systems may make treatment-resistant cancer cells more vulnerable to destruction. Experimental studies have demonstrated interactions between ferroptosis and apoptosis. For example, sanguinarine, a plant-derived compound, has been shown to activate both pathways in cervical cancer cells through increased reactive oxygen species (ROS). Inhibiting either pathway can affect the other, suggesting that coordinated activation may strengthen anticancer effects. However, these findings remain preclinical. The tumor microenvironment also influences ferroptosis. Research discussed in the review shows that tumor-associated macrophages can release extracellular vesicles carrying microRNAs that suppress lipid peroxidation pathways, helping cancer cells resist ferroptotic death. Understanding these interactions could reveal additional ways to overcome treatment resistance. Other important mechanisms include pyroptosis and necroptosis, two inflammatory forms of programmed cell death. Pyroptosis involves inflammasome activation, inflammatory caspases and gasdermin proteins that form pores in cell membranes. Necroptosis involves signaling through RIPK1, RIPK3 and MLKL, ultimately causing membrane disruption. These pathways have complex effects on cancer. Under certain conditions, they eliminate malignant cells and stimulate antitumor immune responses. However, persistent inflammatory signaling may also promote tumor growth or immune suppression. Their therapeutic value therefore depends on the biological context and how selectively they can be activated. The review also discusses PANoptosis, an integrated cell death process involving interactions among pyroptosis, apoptosis and necroptosis. Although investigated in several cancer models, direct evidence in cervical cancer remains limited. Further research is needed to determine whether activating these pathways together could improve treatment outcomes. Autophagy represents another important regulator of cellular survival and death. This process allows cells to recycle damaged proteins and organelles. In cervical cancer, autophagy may protect tumor cells during metabolic stress, but it can also facilitate apoptosis or ferroptosis by influencing iron availability, lipid metabolism and mitochondrial function. These opposing effects make autophagy difficult to target. Drugs such as chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine have been investigated as autophagy modulators in combination treatments, but their clinical effectiveness for this purpose in cervical cancer remains uncertain. The review further examines cuproptosis, a copper-dependent form of regulated cell death associated with mitochondrial protein dysfunction. Preclinical research suggests that manipulating copper-dependent pathways may increase chemotherapy sensitivity. For example, baicalein combined with cisplatin has shown effects involving apoptosis and cuproptosis-related signaling in cervical cancer models. Additional mechanisms include parthanatos, associated with excessive PARP1 activation following DNA damage; lysosome-dependent cell death, involving the release of destructive lysosomal enzymes; and NETosis, which involves neutrophil extracellular traps that can influence inflammation and metastasis. These pathways offer further research opportunities, although therapeutic applications remain less developed. Beyond directly eliminating cancer cells, programmed cell death also influences tumor immunity. HPV-associated tumors may evade immune surveillance by altering antigen presentation, interferon signaling and immune checkpoint pathways, including PD-1/PD-L1. These changes can reduce the ability of immune cells to recognize and destroy malignant cells. An important concept is immunogenic cell death (ICD), in which dying cancer cells release signals that stimulate antitumor immunity. Molecules such as ATP and HMGB1, together with calreticulin exposure on the cell surface, can promote dendritic cell activation and help initiate cytotoxic T-cell responses. This creates opportunities to combine cell death-inducing treatments with immunotherapy. The review discusses strategies involving ferroptosis-inducing agents, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and immune checkpoint inhibitors. While PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors already have an established role in selected patients with cervical cancer, combining them with experimental cell death modulators requires further investigation. The article also highlights potential molecular biomarkers for treatment selection. Gene-expression signatures associated with ferroptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis and immunogenic cell death have shown associations with patient survival and immune characteristics. However, most require prospective validation before they can reliably guide clinical decisions. Another proposed direction involves targeting HPV E6 and E7 to restore sensitivity to multiple cell death pathways. Combining these approaches with ferroptosis modulators, PARP-targeted treatments or immunotherapy could potentially improve antitumor responses, although these strategies require direct experimental testing. “Overall, the future of PCD research in cervical cancer lies not in identifying additional death pathways, but in strategically integrating them into precision oncology frameworks.” The review emphasizes that translating these findings into clinical practice will require more sophisticated experimental models and validated biomarkers. Three-dimensional tumor organoids, patient-derived models and systems incorporating immune and stromal cells may help researchers better understand how interconnected cell death pathways function within tumors. Important challenges remain. Many proposed interventions have been tested primarily in cell lines or animal models, while some mechanistic evidence comes from other cancer types. Excessive activation of inflammatory or oxidative pathways may damage healthy tissues, and difficulties involving drug delivery, systemic toxicity and tumor heterogeneity complicate clinical development. As a narrative review, the article does not present new experimental findings or a quantitative meta-analysis. The available evidence varies in quality and clinical relevance, and many proposed treatment combinations have not been adequately evaluated in humans. Well-designed clinical studies will be essential to determine whether targeting these pathways improves treatment response, survival or other meaningful outcomes. Overall, the review highlights programmed cell death as an interconnected network linking HPV-mediated cancer development, immune regulation and treatment resistance. Rather than focusing exclusively on apoptosis, the findings support investigating multiple interacting cell death mechanisms as potential therapeutic targets. Integrating these insights with validated biomarkers and existing treatments may eventually contribute to more individualized and effective cervical cancer care. news.title_zh: HPV驱动的细胞死亡途径为宫颈癌 治疗提供了新方向 - EurekAlert!
news.source_body_en: A new review published in Oncoscience on September 30, 2026, titled 'Programmed cell death pathways in cervical cancer: Cross-talk, HPV-mediated regulation, and therapeutic implications: A narrative review' explores how human papillomavirus (HPV) alters programmed cell death (PCD) pathways in cervical cancer. The study emphasizes that HPV, particularly high-risk types like HPV16 and HPV18, contributes to treatment resistance by suppressing apoptosis through viral proteins E6 and E7. It also discusses other PCD mechanisms, such as ferroptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis, and PANoptosis, which may offer alternative therapeutic strategies. However, most findings are preclinical, and further research is needed to validate their clinical relevance. The review highlights the importance of understanding these pathways to improve treatment outcomes for cervical cancer patients.

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer High-risk HPV common among asymptomatic rural Ugandan women by October 26, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 High-risk HPV common among asymptomatic rural Ugandan women Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A cross-sectional study of 7,126 women aged 30–49 years in rural Uganda found that 1,800, or 25.3%, tested positive for high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV). Among the positive women with complete genotype data, infections outside the HPV16 and HPV18 groups were common, while a comparison of genotype groups with clinical assessment found no statistically significant relationship with visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) outcome. The study focused on asymptomatic women who self-collected vaginal samples for testing with the GeneXpert HPV assay. The investigators recorded the presence or absence of specific hrHPV genotypes and used the results to describe genotype distribution in this rural population. All hrHPV-positive participants were invited to receive visual assessment for treatment, with or without VIA, and were treated according to the assessment. No histopathology was performed, so the clinical observations were not accompanied by a histological characterization of cervical lesions. Complete genotype information was available for 1,422 of the 1,800 hrHPV-positive participants. The largest individual genotype group was HPV31/33/35/52/58, detected in 324 women, or 22.8% of those with complete results. Multiple genotypes were the most frequent category, occurring in 397 women, or 27.9%. The remaining distribution consisted of HPV39/56/66/68 in 243 women, or 17.1%; HPV16 in 183, or 12.9%; HPV18/45 in 161, or 11.3%; and HPV51/59 in 114, or 8.0%. These figures show that the detected infections were not confined to HPV16 and HPV18 and that multiple hrHPV genotypes were frequently present. Of the 1,121 hrHPV-positive women who underwent VIA, irrespective of genotype, 159, or 14.2%, had a positive inspection. Eight women, equal to 0.7% of those inspected, were identified as having cervical cancer. Six of these women were positive for HPV31/33/35/52/58, with three also positive for HPV16, HPV51/59, or HPV39/56/66/68. One woman was positive for HPV18/45, and one was HPV16-positive with an unknown additional genotype. The analysis found no statistically significant relationship between genotype and VIA outcome, meaning the study did not establish a statistical association between the genotype categories and the result of the inspection in the population examined. The findings support the authors’ conclusion that the study population had a high prevalence of non-16/18 hrHPV and that extended genotyping may be relevant to managing women at risk for cervical cancer in Uganda. The eight cervical cancers were identified within the smaller group of hrHPV-positive women who underwent VIA; the figures therefore describe findings in that clinical subgroup and should not be read as population-wide cervical-cancer incidence or direct estimates of genotype-specific risk. The authors call for additional research on the possible role of HPV31/33/35/52/58 in cervical carcinogenesis and on whether available vaccines protect the population against the broader range of hrHPV genotypes found in the study. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health HPV Clades and Age Sharpen Risk Prediction for High-Grade Lesions in AGC-NOS by October 29, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 HPV Clades and Age Sharpen Risk Prediction for High-Grade Lesions in AGC-NOS Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective study of 588 patients with atypical glandular cells, not otherwise specified (AGC-NOS), suggests that the phylogenetic clade of an infecting high-risk HPV type, together with patient age and infection multiplicity, can stratify the risk of precancerous or worse lesions. The research, conducted at the International Peace Maternal and Child Health Hospital, School of Medicine, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, was published in Diagnostic Pathology and is presented as preliminary evidence pending external validation. The new analysis set out to characterize age, HPV clade distribution and multiple infections in this population, and to build a refined risk prediction model. The researchers reviewed records from January 2019 to December 2023. All 588 patients had undergone liquid-based cytology and testing for 14 high-risk HPV genotypes, followed by histopathologic evaluation. Precancerous or worse lesions were identified in 9.5% of patients (56 of 588), and the overall high-risk HPV positivity rate was 17.7% (104 of 588). The Alpha-9 and Alpha-7 clades were significantly enriched among patients who had outcome lesions compared with those who did not: 19.6% versus 8.3% for Alpha-9, and 17.9% versus 1.5% for Alpha-7. In multivariable analysis, Alpha-7 emerged as the strongest independent predictor, with an odds ratio of 20.43 (95% confidence interval: 7.22–60.07). Alpha-9 carried an odds ratio of 3.41 (95% CI: 1.43–7.57), and each additional year of age raised the odds by a factor of 1.04 (95% CI: 1.01–1.07). The model also incorporated infection multiplicity and AGC subtype. Performance was moderate rather than definitive. The model showed acceptable discrimination, with an area under the curve of 0.74 (95% CI: 0.66–0.82), and good calibration. Discrimination of 0.74 indicates meaningful but imperfect separation of patients who develop lesions from those who do not, leaving room for refinement. When patients were sorted into risk groups, observed lesion rates rose in a graded fashion: 4.5% (8 of 176) in the low-risk group, 8.2% (30 of 364) in the intermediate-risk group, and 37.5% (18 of 48) in the high-risk group, with a P for trend of 6.7 × 10−8. This gradient suggests the model captures real differences in risk across the cohort. The authors concluded that a model incorporating HPV phylogenetic clades, age, infection multiplicity and AGC subtype provided preliminary evidence of potential value for risk stratification in AGC-NOS, with the Alpha-7 clade as the strongest independent predictor. They emphasized that pending external validation, this approach may support more individualized management of patients with AGC-NOS. Several limitations frame these findings. The study was retrospective and single-center, and its results derive from one hospital’s patient population over a five-year period. The reported odds ratios and risk-group rates describe associations within this cohort and do not by themselves establish that clade testing improves clinical outcomes. The authors themselves flag external validation as a prerequisite before the model could inform practice. Within those limits, the work adds a specific technical angle to HPV-based cervical cancer risk assessment: rather than treating all high-risk HPV infections alike, it distinguishes between phylogenetic clades, finding that Alpha-7 types carried a markedly higher association with precancerous or worse lesions in this AGC-NOS population. If validated in independent cohorts, such clade-level information could help identify which patients with this ambiguous cytological result warrant the closest follow-up. supplementary_news.content: Skip to content All Regions All Regions BioHealth Capital Region Greater Philadelphia Research Triangle Park News Events Jobs For Employers Sponsorship Log In Sign Up Log In Sign Up North CarolinaIndustry TrendsResearch Waters and Labcorp to Expand Access to Cervical Cancer Screening with the Most Comprehensive FDA-Approved HPV Testing Option Beginning in Late 2026 Published October 30, 2026 · 5 min read · North Carolina ← News / Waters and Labcorp to Expand Access to Cervical... Labcorp intends to be the first commercial laboratory to offer FDA-approved HPV testing with the BD OnclarityTM HPV Assay across clinician-collected and self-collected screening options in clinic, patient service center, and at-home settings Through a network serving more than 850,000 physicians and healthcare providers and more than 2,200 patient service centers, Labcorp is helping expand access to cervical cancer screening nationwide First and only FDA-approved HPV test that supports all ASCCP Enduring Risk-Based Management Guidelines by providing comprehensive extended genotyping MILFORD, Mass. and BURLINGTON, N.C., Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Labcorp (NYSE: LH), a global leader of innovative and comprehensive laboratory services, and Waters Corporation (NYSE: WAT), a global life sciences and diagnostics leader, today announced a partnership to expand access to the FDA-approved BD Onclarity HPV Assay through Labcorp’s nationwide laboratory network beginning in late 2026. Cervical cancer is largely preventable through routine screening and early detection of human papillomavirus (HPV), yet millions of women remain overdue for recommended tests. This collaboration is designed to help address persistent cervical cancer screening gaps by bringing more accessible screening options to patients across the United States. Labcorp will provide these HPV testing options to support its clinician programs, Gaps in Care health plan programs, and Labcorp OnDemand consumer channel.2-8 “Barriers such as privacy, access, and socioeconomic factors can make it difficult to stay current with cervical cancer screening,” said Jeff Andrews, M.D., FRCSC, Vice President of Medical Affairs, Waters Advanced Diagnostics, Waters Corporation.5-7 “We are at the start of a new era in which screening can extend beyond the clinic, enable more personalized risk assessment, and reach people who have historically been underserved. By offering greater flexibility in how and where people are screened, our collaboration marks a critical step forward in bridging one of today’s most profound care gaps.” The Most Comprehensive FDA-Approved HPV Testing Option The BD Onclarity HPV Assay is the only FDA-approved HPV test that supports all American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP) Enduring Risk-Based Management Guidelines.2,9 “Cervical cancer screening saves lives, but too many women still face barriers to getting screened,” said Dr. Brian Caveney, Chief Medical and Scientific Officer, Labcorp. “By expanding access and options for comprehensive FDA-approved HPV testing, we can help more women stay current with recommended screening, reach those who may be overdue for care, and support earlier identification of cervical cancer risk.” Certain HPV genotypes, including types 16, 18 and 45, are associated with an increased risk of cervical cancer, making genotype-specific information important for patient management.9 As HPV vaccination has reduced infections from HPV types 16 and 18, other high-risk HPV strains now account for a growing share of cervical disease, particularly among younger, vaccinated populations.10 The BD Onclarity HPV Assay offers extended genotyping that individually identifies HPV types 16, 18, 31, 45, 51 and 52 along with three sets of strategically pooled results, regardless of collection method, making it the most comprehensive HPV screening tool available in the U.S. today.2,11 Waters and Labcorp intend to offer the BD Onclarity HPV Assay by the end of 2026. supplementary_news.content_title: HPV prevention, local action drive push for a cervical cancer-free Philippines
supplementary_news.content: CERVICAL cancer is one of the few cancers the world has set out to eliminate as a public health problem. For the Philippines, however, reaching that goal will depend not only on national targets but on whether prevention actually reaches girls and women in their communities. At the center of prevention is the human papillomavirus (HPV), a common virus transmitted through sexual contact. While most HPV infections clear on their own, persistent infection with high-risk HPV types can lead to cervical cancer. Around 95 percent of cervical cancer cases are linked to persistent high-risk HPV infection, making HPV vaccination an important opportunity to prevent the disease before it develops, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The WHO has set a 90-70-90 strategy toward cervical cancer elimination by 2030: 90 percent of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15, 70 percent of women screened with a high-performance test by ages 35 and 45, and 90 percent of women identified with cervical disease receiving treatment. At the recent Association of Municipal Health Officers of the Philippines symposium on “Leading Disease Prevention at the Local Level: The Role of LGUs in Protecting Communities,” health experts brought the global target closer to home: how can proven prevention measures translate into protection that people can actually access in their barangays, municipalities and cities? Closing the gaps in HPV vaccination Get the latest news delivered to your inbox Sign up for The Manila Times newsletters By signing up with an email address, I acknowledge that I have read and agree to the Terms of Service and Privacy Policy . Pediatric Infectious Disease Specialist Dr. Fejelia Faulan, resource speaker and panelist, emphasized that gaps in HPV vaccination cannot be traced to one factor alone. Families, health care providers, schools and communities can all influence whether eligible children ultimately receive protection. ADVOCATING HPV VACCINATION Dr. Fejelia Faulan discusses the role of HPV vaccination and stronger local implementation in accelerating the Philippines’ progress toward cervical cancer elimination. “The gaps are on many sides,” Faulan said, pointing to challenges ranging from parental and community attitudes to vaccine access and hesitancy. She noted that misinformation and resistance to vaccination can make reaching eligible populations particularly difficult. Another important gap is data. While government vaccination programs capture vaccinations delivered through the public sector, Faulan noted that there is no comprehensive national registry capturing HPV vaccination delivered through private practice. In Western Visayas, members of the Philippine Pediatric Society have started gathering vaccination information from private practitioners, which Faulan said could help provide a more complete picture of coverage. “We started that program because we wanted to share our data with the government; so that we can address and minimize the gap,” Faulan said. “We hope that there will be others, other municipalities who will join, so that it can become national data for private practitioners.” The issue goes beyond measurement. If local governments do not know how many children have already been vaccinated through private clinics and schools, it becomes harder to identify who is still being missed and where resources should be directed. Faulan also underscored the importance of widening vaccination reach. The current government program prioritizes girls aged 9 to 14, but she noted that HPV infection is not exclusively a concern for women. HPV can also cause cancers affecting men, including anal, penile and oropharyngeal cancers. WHO likewise recognizes HPV as a cause of several cancers beyond cervical cancer. Local success stories show that ambitious vaccination targets are achievable. During the symposium, Faulan highlighted areas that have reached the 90 percent HPV vaccination target, including Banna in Ilocos Norte and Sampaloc, Quezon, while Ilocos Norte subsequently achieved the target province-wide. “If Ilocos Norte has done this, and one municipality in Quezon has done this, I think we can do this,” Faulan told local health leaders. Making prevention a sustained local priority For Dr. Debra Maria Catulong, city health officer of Mandaue City and Best-Practice Panelist, closing the gap requires LGUs to shift their thinking from detecting disease to preventing it in the first place. “Why are we waiting for people to get sick and diagnose or screen? Why can’t we do something before that?” Catulong said, describing Mandaue City's move toward prevention under the primary healthcare approach. CERVICAL CANCER PREVENTION Dr. Debra Maria Catulong shares Mandaue City’s approach to strengthening cervical cancer prevention through local planning, sustainable financing and expanded HPV vaccination.PHOTO FROM The city is putting this into practice through a cervical cancer prevention initiative designed to complement the national program. While government-supplied HPV vaccines reach eligible girls through the public sector, Mandaue City has allocated local resources to extend vaccination to girls aged 9 to 14 in private schools, helping address a population that may otherwise be missed. The city is also working to establish a mechanism for capturing private-sector vaccination data to better understand its actual coverage. For Catulong, however, vaccination campaigns should not become one-time activities. Sustainable prevention requires LGUs to formally incorporate cervical cancer elimination into their annual plans and identify resources that can support implementation over time. Mandaue City, for instance, is augmenting its health budget through several sources, including its general fund, Special Health Fund and Gender and Development Fund. “Marami kayong pwedeng ma-source out na funds. Ang importante lang, the willingness, awareness and acknowledgement na gusto mong ipasok ’yan na budget should be coming from us,” Catulong told municipal health officers. She added that local strategies should combine vaccination with health promotion and navigation for patients already diagnosed, while tapping private companies, civil society organizations and other partners within the community. “It should be something that’s sustainable. As much as possible, embed it in the plans annually,” Catulong said. “Hindi kaya ito ng isang sektor lang. We all need to work together if we really want to eliminate cervical cancer.” That approach reflects one of the central lessons emerging from the symposium: national targets become meaningful only when they are translated into local plans, budgets and services. Science has already established a pathway toward cervical cancer elimination. Closing the remaining gap will increasingly depend on knowing who is still being missed, making vaccination accessible across public and private settings, sustaining local financing and building partnerships that can carry prevention beyond individual campaigns. For LGUs, the opportunity is to turn the 90-70-90 targets from national numbers into something more tangible: girls protected from HPV today, and fewer women facing cervical cancer in the years ahead

supplementary_news.content_title: More Adolescents Starting HPV Vaccine Series at Age 9-10 Finish It by Age 13 Than if Starting Later
supplementary_news.content: Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More EN RegisterLog In Ask AI Search AI Mode Medscape Medical NewsConference News More Adolescents Starting HPV Vaccine Series at Age 9-10 Finish It by Age 13 Than if Starting Later Tara Haelle October 27, 2026 1 Add to Email Alerts Jump to Key Points WASHINGTON — Children whose pediatricians recommended initiating the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination series at ages 9-10 had over twice the odds of starting and completing the series by age 13 than those whose pediatricians initiated the series at ages 11-12, according to a cluster randomized controlled trial presented at IDWeek 2026 in Washington, DC on October 22. “We also found that earlier introduction seems to make HPV vaccine conversations shorter and easier,” Sean T. O’Leary, MD, MPH, professor of pediatrics at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and Children’s Hospital Colorado in Aurora, told attendees. “Clinicians currently recommending HPV vaccine at 11 or older should consider earlier introduction, and policymakers should consider a preferential recommendation for earlier introduction of HPV vaccine at 9-10 years.” Currently, HPV vaccination is one of the rare circumstances where the recommendation from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) differs slightly from that of the CDC, O’Leary said. The CDC recommends the HPV vaccine series begin at age 11 or 12 but noted it can be started as early as age 9. The AAP, meanwhile, recommends starting the series between ages 9 and 12, “at an age the pediatric health care professional deems optimal for acceptance and completion of the vaccination series,” according to the 2018 Red Book. Previous evidence has suggested better uptake of the HPV vaccine when the series is started sooner, but those studies are mostly retrospective, observational studies, and only a small proportion, 2%-8% of adolescents, had initiated the series early. No data existed on the reasons for those early initiation cases, and it’s possible that there are differences between providers who vaccinate earlier vs later, O’Leary said. Similarly, past quality improvement studies that initiated the series earlier generally involved multiple interventions instead of focusing only on an earlier start to the HPV vaccination series. O’Leary noted several reasons it’s worth considering starting the HPV series at age 9, including more opportunities to vaccinate before exposure and a more robust immune response at younger ages. Starting earlier also allows for spreading out the number of shots youth receive since they would then receive fewer shots at age 11, when they are also recommended to get the Tdap and meningitis ACWY (MenACWY) vaccines as well as their annual flu vaccine. Some reports have also suggested that earlier initiation of the HPV vaccine helps uncouple discussions of sexuality from the shot “and allow a better focus on cancer prevention for early introduction,” O’Leary said. “We also know that antibody levels from HPV vaccination are they’re really well sustained, and they plateau for at least 15 years, probably longer.” SUGGESTED FOR YOU The study involved 31 pediatric practices in Colorado and California that currently initiated the HPV vaccine series at ages 11-12. The study randomly assigned 16 of those practices, with 106 clinicians, to receive a training module for clinicians and staff to improve HPV vaccination with specific guidance on wording for parents about starting the series at ages 9-10. The other 15 practices, with 112 clinicians, also received training on improving HPV vaccination but without the specific guidance about ages 9-10. Both arms had Zoom calls annually with feedback on missed HPV vaccinations at visits. The practices’ populations were similar at baseline, with about one fifth of patients on Medicaid and 28% of patients aged 9-13 years up to date on their HPV vaccine series. During the study, the arm focused on earlier initiation had 28,407 patients ever aged 9-13 years, and the control arm had 33,839 patients ever aged 9-13 years. The median age at initiation and completion of the series was 11 and 12 years, respectively, in the age 9-10 arm and 11 and 13 in the age 11-12 arm. Over the course of the study from 2021 to 2026, more adolescents in the age 9-10 arm had initiated the HPV vaccine series by age 13 than in the age 11-12 arm (77.2% vs 67%; adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 2.19; P < .001). Similarly, 61.7% of adolescents in the age 9-10 arm had completed the series by age 13 compared to 45.1% in the age 11-12 arm (aHR, 2.37; P < .001). Adolescents in the age 9-10 arm initiated the series at a median age of 11 years and completed it at a median age of 11.8 years, compared with a median age of 12.2 years at initiation and 13.3 years at completion in the age 11-12 arm. About 3 months after starting the study, the researchers conducted interviews with 18 clinicians and 17 office staff workers in the age 9-10 arm. They found that many parents seemed receptive to vaccination at ages 9-10, and discussions about the vaccine at these ages appeared shorter with less mention of sexual activity. The main pushback they experienced came from having expected a shot-free visit. “Parents had told the kids they didn’t think they were getting any shots that visit, but lo and behold, yes, they were,” O’Leary said. “Parental questions, concerns, and hesitancy didn’t really appear to differ between the study arms,” nor did the perceived ability to convince parents to get the shot. The clinicians also liked that they could spread out the shots instead of giving them all at one visit. “There was some concern that if you do this in an early visit, maybe they’ll skip later well-child visits,” O’Leary said, but that didn’t happen. “We didn’t see any difference in the percentage of children receiving well-child visits between the study arms, and we also didn’t see a difference in the percentage of adolescents who were up to date on the MenACWY and Tdap vaccines by age 13.” It’s not clear how generalizable to the study might be to states outside California and Colorado or in rural areas since the study clinics were all urban or suburban, O’Leary said. The results of the study were encouraging if not all that surprising, Simon Parzen-Johnson, MD, professor of pediatrics at the University of Chicago and Comer Children’s Hospital in Chicago, told Medscape Medical News. “Most of the conventions that we have in terms of age are somewhat arbitrary, and I think that reassessing and figuring out when the right time is to do things is always a good idea,” said Parzen-Johnson, who was not involved in the research. During O’Leary’s presentation, Parzen-Johnson had asked whether there might be concerns about recommending earlier initiation of the HPV vaccine series in the current climate of increased vaccine hesitancy in the US. O’Leary acknowledged the problems with vaccine hesitancy and confusion about vaccines but pointed out that more than 90% of parents still vaccinate their children on time according to the recommended immunization schedule. While HPV vaccination rates remain suboptimal and have plateaued, they have not declined in the midst of ongoing chaos in the national vaccine conversation, and he doesn’t see a reason for that to change how pediatricians practice. It will take a while to find out how the lawsuit between the AAP and Kennedy resolves and what happens with the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), “so it’s going to be quite a while before we have a functioning ACIP that can be trusted,” he said. “But right now, AAP is taking on these recommendations for adolescents and working with other professional societies.” Parzen-Johnson agrees that current national concerns about vaccine hesitancy should not necessarily affect how individual doctors interact with their patients one-on-one. “Care of children in my mind hasn’t changed from a clinician standpoint, and our goal is always to provide whatever the best care is possible, regardless of what’s going on at a national level, international level, or local level, so I think you can always come back to that,” Parzen-Johnson said. He tells parents that, as a pediatrician, his goal has always remained the same — to take care of their child. “Regardless of what’s going outside of that, we’re always going to be striving to figure out what the best way to do that is,” he said. “So, yes, there’s a lot of noise [in the national discourse], but maybe we should continue to make this about me and you, in this room, talking about your child.” The research was funded by the National Cancer Institute. O’Leary had no disclosures. Tara Haelle has been an independent science and health journalist for more than 15 years, with work appearing in over two dozen trade and consumer publications. She is the author of Vaccination Investigation: The History and Science of Vaccines and The Informed Parent: A Science-Based Resource for Your Child’s First Four Years. Haelle is the public health beat leader for the Association of Health Care Journalists, where she develops resources to help other journalists report on medical studies and public health.
